title: Picot cast-on
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 348, 'Casting on with picots'. Public domain. The method is also described in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s series). Public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: The action of closing live stitches so they cannot unravel, worked by passing one stitch over another along the needle. Called 'bind off' in US terminology.
A cast-off method that mirrors the picot cast-on, adding small decorative loops along the final edge of a piece.

content.text: The picot cast-on works by casting on a small group of stitches. A
cast-off

closes the group into a tiny loop. The process repeats so each loop forms one decorative point along the edge. The points are locked closed before the next group starts, so they sit firmly and will not unravel if the edge is pulled.

You need yarn, needles, and the ability to work both a knitted-on cast-on and a basic cast-off. A crochet hook one or two sizes smaller than your knitting needles is a useful aid for returning stitches if you drop one.

attrs.title: Fig. 348, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (Therese de Dillmont, 1886). Public domain.

content.text: Step by step
The following works a picot every 4 stitches. Adjust the grouping to vary the size and spacing of the points.
Make a slip knot and place it on the left needle.
Using the knitted-on cast-on, cast on 4 more stitches. You have 5 stitches total on the left needle.
Cast off 2 of those stitches: knit 2, then pass the first stitch over the second. One stitch remains on the right needle.
Transfer this remaining stitch back to the left needle. The small closed loop sitting below the needle is the first picot.
Cast on 4 more stitches using the knitted-on method. Cast off 2. Transfer the remaining stitch to the left needle. This makes the second picot.
Repeat step 5 until you have the required number of stitches, ending after a transfer step rather than mid-group.
Count the stitches on the needle (not the picot loops below) and begin the first row of your pattern.
Where you'll see it

The picot cast-on appears on the cast-on edge of baby garments, shawl borders, and lace scarves where a plain cast-on edge would be too severe. It is also used at cuff edges and along the lower hem of fine-weight garments to add a small decorative detail that survives washing.
Common faults

Picot loops pulling tight. The cast-off of 2 should be worked at the same tension as the rest of the cast-on. If you tighten automatically when casting off, the loops will be visibly smaller than they should be. Try working the cast-off stitches on a needle one size larger.

Stitch count off after each picot group. Because you cast on and then cast off within the same group, the count on the needle can feel confusing. Count only the stitches currently sitting on the needle; don't include the picot loops hanging below.
Uneven spacing between picots. This is usually caused by varying the number of stitches in each group. Keep a tally mark for each group as you work.
What to try next: apply the same picot idea to a cast-off edge to get a matching
picot cast-off
. This gives matching start and finish edges on shawls and lace collars.
